frase_gancho.texto: A young man peers out from between the jaws of a stone eagle.

puente_narrativo.texto: So far, war and the Sun. Now the tone shifts: look for a young seated god, his body covered in flowers and plants carved in stone.

guion_corto.texto: This stone head, about thirty centimeters tall, shows a young man whose face looks out from between the open jaws of an eagle-shaped helmet. Notice his expression: serene, steady, almost calm. He is an eagle knight, a member of one of the most prestigious military orders in the Mexica army. To get there, you had to earn it on the battlefield by capturing live prisoners. The eagle represented the Sun, the day and the strength of the sky; its opposite partner, the jaguar, represented the night and the underworld. The sculptor took great care with the human face so that the helmet would not hide the man, but show him transformed into a bird.

guion_largo.texto:
This is the head that was promised to you a few halls back: a human face emerging from the jaws of an eagle helmet. The Mexica sculptors did not carve an eagle; they carved a man inside the eagle. The beak sits above, like a visor, and the jaws frame the face. This was not a party costume, but the dress uniform of the most feared warriors, made of feathers and other materials, which made them look like birds of prey. In battle, the effect they sought was terror.

How did one become one of them? The Mexica military career worked by merit. A young man began by accompanying an experienced warrior, and to move up he needed to capture live prisoners, not just kill. According to some versions, at least four captives were needed to earn the right to dress as an eagle or a jaguar. A farmer’s son could go far with courage, but a nobleman’s son also had to prove himself.

Capturing alive had a religious reason. That prisoner would go to sacrifice to feed the Sun, as on the [Stone of Tízoc](mna_s06_tizoc) or the jaguar you have just seen. That is why the one who captured was admired more than the one who killed. On the Stone of Tízoc, moreover, the defeated do not appear dead, but seized by the hair: not destroyed, but captured.

For those who died in combat, or on the sacrificial stone, the Mexica imagined a glorious fate. It was believed that warriors accompanied the Sun from dawn until midday, and that after four years they returned to the world transformed into hummingbirds and butterflies. Remember the butterfly on the chest of the [Atlante de Tula](mna_s05_atlante_tula), or the butterflies on the brazier from Teotihuacán. And that is why the god of war, Huitzilopochtli, whose name is interpreted as “left-handed hummingbird” or “hummingbird of the south,” was also the patron of fallen warriors.

If you want to see what one would look like in full figure, you can visit the Templo Mayor Museum afterward, in the Historic Center. In 1981, next to the Templo Mayor, in a building called the House of the Eagles, two nearly life-size figures of baked clay were found, representing warriors wearing eagle helmets. It is thought that this building was a meeting place for the warrior elite, just steps from the sacred heart of Tenochtitlan.

When you look at this head again, notice what is missing: it has no look of fury and no clenched teeth. It has serenity. Perhaps because in the Mexica mind the warrior did not act out of hatred, but out of duty: an entire life devoted to keeping the Sun on its path. It is a very different image from the one we usually have of war.

And if you are looking for the echo of this image in another hall, remember the frieze of Tula: there the royal eagles held hearts between their talons. Here, the eagle becomes a person. It is the same animal, the same idea, but now with a face. And from this comes the name of the vessels you have just seen: cuauhxicalli, “eagle vessel,” where the eagle is at once the Sun and the warrior.

texto: Find the eagle’s beak above the young man’s forehead
Look at his face: what expression does it have?
Find the feathers carved around the helmet

texto.Dimensions: 32 cm high x 30 cm wide x 26 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: Only nobles could become eagle warriors.
texto.respuesta: Reality: According to the chronicles, a commoner could also become one if he captured enough prisoners; war was one of the few paths to advancement.
